contentHtml:
USA—Roche secured FDA approval for Gazyva (obinutuzumab) to treat primary membranous nephropathy (pMN), expanding the drug’s use in autoimmune diseases as the pharmaceutical company seeks new growth opportunities beyond blood cancer.

The approval makes Gazyva the first treatment specifically approved by the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) for adults with pMN to reduce proteinuria, an abnormal level of protein in urine that indicates damage to the kidneys.

The rare autoimmune disease occurs when the immune system mistakenly attacks the kidneys’ filtering structures, potentially impairing their ability to remove waste from the blood.

“pMN can lead to debilitating physical and psychological symptoms that place a heavy burden on patients, families and healthcare systems alike,” said Teresa Graham, CEO of Roche Pharmaceuticals, in a November 16 statement.

She added that the approval provides a targeted treatment option for patients and expands Gazyva’s potential in immune-mediated kidney diseases.

Clinical trial results support approval

The FDA based its decision on results from the phase 3 Majesty trial, which compared Gazyva with tacrolimus, an immunosuppressant commonly used to manage autoimmune conditions.

After two years of treatment, 36.1% of patients receiving Gazyva achieved complete remission of proteinuria, compared with 5.7% of those taking tacrolimus.

Complete remission required a urine protein-to-creatinine ratio of no more than 0.3 g/g, stable estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR), and no rescue treatment, treatment failure or early discontinuation.

The treatment advantage persisted through week 76, when complete remission rates remained at 36.1% for Gazyva and 8.6% for tacrolimus.

These results demonstrated the drug’s ability to reduce protein loss through the kidneys over an extended treatment period.

Roche expands Gazyva’s autoimmune portfolio

The pMN approval represents another step in Roche’s strategy to expand Gazyva beyond oncology.

The drug is already approved for certain blood cancers, lupus nephritis and idiopathic nephrotic syndrome.

Roche is also awaiting an FDA decision, expected by December 4, 2026, on a potential indication for systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE).

The company has projected peak sales of CHF 2 billion (US$2.5 billion) from Gazyva’s autoimmune disease indications, reflecting its expectations for the growing role of the drug in immunology.

However, competition in chronic lymphocytic leukaemia and follicular lymphoma continues to affect its overall commercial performance.

Gazyva generated CHF 751 million (US$946 million) in sales during the first nine months of 2026, representing 7% growth year over year at constant exchange rates.

Roche plans to report Gazyva sales separately by therapeutic area in future financial updates, providing greater visibility into the contribution of its oncology and autoimmune disease businesses.
